L34: ## File Names, Command Line Arguments, and Environment Variables【20†¶】
L35: 
L36: In Python, file names, command line arguments, and environment variables are represented using the string type. On some systems, decoding these strings to and from bytes is necessary before passing them to the operating system. Python uses the 【21†filesystem encoding and error handler】 to perform this conversion (see 【22†`sys.getfilesystemencoding()`】).
L37: The 【21†filesystem encoding and error handler】 are configured at Python startup by the 【23†`PyConfig_Read()`】 function: see 【24†`filesystem_encoding`】 and 【25†`filesystem_errors`】 members of 【26†`PyConfig`】.
L38: Changed in version 3.1: On some systems, conversion using the file system encoding may fail. In this case, Python uses the 【27†surrogateescape encoding error handler】, which means that undecodable bytes are replaced by a Unicode character U+DCxx on decoding, and these are again translated to the original byte on encoding.
L39: The 【21†file system encoding】 must guarantee to successfully decode all bytes below 128. If the file system encoding fails to provide this guarantee, API functions can raise 【28†`UnicodeError`】.
L40: 
L41: See also the 【29†locale encoding】.
L42: ## Python UTF-8 Mode【30†¶】
L43: 
L44: Added in version 3.7: See 【31†PEP 540†peps.python.org】 for more details.
L45: 
L46: Changed in version 3.15: Python UTF-8 mode is now enabled by default (【32†PEP 686†peps.python.org】). It may be disabled by setting 【33†`PYTHONUTF8=0`】 as an environment variable or by using the 【34†`-X utf8=0`】 command line option.
L47: 
L48: The Python UTF-8 Mode ignores the 【29†locale encoding】 and forces the usage of the UTF-8 encoding:
L49: 
L50:   * Use UTF-8 as the 【21†filesystem encoding】.
L51:   * 【22†`sys.getfilesystemencoding()`】 returns `'utf-8'`.
L52: 
L53:   * 【35†`locale.getpreferredencoding()`】 returns `'utf-8'` (the do_setlocale argument has no effect).
L54: 
L55:   * 【36†`sys.stdin`】, 【37†`sys.stdout`】, and 【38†`sys.stderr`】 all use UTF-8 as their text encoding, with the `surrogateescape` 【39†error handler】 being enabled for `sys.stdin` and `sys.stdout` (`sys.stderr` continues to use `backslashreplace` as it does in the default locale-aware mode)
L56:   * On Unix, 【40†`os.device_encoding()`】 returns `'utf-8'` rather than the device encoding.
L57: 
L58: Note that the standard stream settings in UTF-8 mode can be overridden by 【41†`PYTHONIOENCODING`】 (just as they can be in the default locale-aware mode).
L59: 
L60: As a consequence of the changes in those lower level APIs, other higher level APIs also exhibit different default behaviours:
L61: 
L62:   * Command line arguments, environment variables and filenames are decoded to text using the UTF-8 encoding.
L63:   * 【42†`os.fsdecode()`】 and 【43†`os.fsencode()`】 use the UTF-8 encoding.
L64: 
L65:   * 【2†`open()`】, 【44†`io.open()`】, and 【45†`codecs.open()`】 use the UTF-8 encoding by default. However, they still use the strict error handler by default so that attempting to open a binary file in text mode is likely to raise an exception rather than producing nonsense data.
L66: The 【46†Python UTF-8 Mode】 is enabled by default. It can be disabled using the 【34†`-X utf8=0`】 command line option or the 【33†`PYTHONUTF8=0`】 environment variable. The Python UTF-8 Mode can only be disabled at Python startup. Its value can be read from 【47†`sys.flags.utf8_mode`】.
L67: If the UTF-8 mode is disabled, the interpreter defaults to using the current locale settings, unless the current locale is identified as a legacy ASCII-based locale (as described for 【48†`PYTHONCOERCECLOCALE`】), and locale coercion is either disabled or fails. In such legacy locales, the interpreter will default to enabling UTF-8 mode unless explicitly instructed not to do so.

L3548: Execute the program file in a new process.
L3549: (Note that the `subprocess` module provides more powerful facilities for spawning new processes and retrieving their results; using that module is preferable to using these functions. Check especially the Replacing Older Functions with the subprocess Module section.)
L3550: If mode is `P_NOWAIT`, this function returns the process id of the new process; if mode is `P_WAIT`, returns the process’s exit code if it exits normally, or `-signal`, where signal is the signal that killed the process. On Windows, the process id will actually be the process handle, so can be used with the `waitpid()` function.
L3551: 
L3552: Note on VxWorks, this function doesn’t return `-signal` when the new process is killed. Instead it raises OSError exception.
L3553: The “l” and “v” variants of the `spawn*` functions differ in how command-line arguments are passed. The “l” variants are perhaps the easiest to work with if the number of parameters is fixed when the code is written; the individual parameters simply become additional parameters to the `spawnl*()` functions. The “v” variants are good when the number of parameters is variable, with the arguments being passed in a list or tuple as the args parameter.
L3554: In either case, the arguments to the child process must start with the name of the command being run.
L3555: The variants which include a second “p” near the end (`spawnlp()`, `spawnlpe()`, `spawnvp()`, and `spawnvpe()`) will use the `PATH` environment variable to locate the program file. When the environment is being replaced (using one of the `spawn*e` variants, discussed in the next paragraph), the new environment is used as the source of the `PATH` variable.
L3556: The other variants, `spawnl()`, `spawnle()`, `spawnv()`, and `spawnve()`, will not use the `PATH` variable to locate the executable; file must contain an appropriate absolute or relative path.
L3557: For `spawnle()`, `spawnlpe()`, `spawnve()`, and `spawnvpe()` (note that these all end in “e”), the env parameter must be a mapping which is used to define the environment variables for the new process (they are used instead of the current process’ environment); the functions `spawnl()`, `spawnlp()`, `spawnv()`, and `spawnvp()` all cause the new process to inherit the environment of the current process.
L3558: Note that keys and values in the env dictionary must be strings; invalid keys or values will cause the function to fail, with a return value of `127`.
L3559: As an example, the following calls to `spawnlp()` and `spawnvpe()` are equivalent:
L3560: 
L3561:     import os
L3562:     os.spawnlp(os.P_WAIT, 'cp', 'cp', 'index.html', '/dev/null')
L3563: 
L3564:     L = ['cp', 'index.html', '/dev/null']
L3565:     os.spawnvpe(os.P_WAIT, 'cp', L, os.environ)

L3594: os.startfile(path[, operation][, arguments][, cwd][, show_cmd])¶
L3595: Start a file with its associated application.
L3596: 
L3597: When operation is not specified, this acts like double-clicking the file in Windows Explorer, or giving the file name as an argument to the start command from the interactive command shell: the file is opened with whatever application (if any) its extension is associated.
L3601: The default working directory is inherited, but may be overridden by the cwd argument. This should be an absolute path. A relative path will be resolved against this argument.
L3602: 
L3603: Use show_cmd to override the default window style. Whether this has any effect will depend on the application being launched. Values are integers as supported by the Win32 `ShellExecute()` function.
L3604: `startfile()` returns as soon as the associated application is launched. There is no option to wait for the application to close, and no way to retrieve the application’s exit status. The path parameter is relative to the current directory or cwd. If you want to use an absolute path, make sure the first character is not a slash (`'/'`) Use `pathlib` or the `os.path.normpath()` function to ensure that paths are properly encoded for Win32.
L3615: Execute the command (a string) in a subshell. This is implemented by calling the Standard C function `system()`, and has the same limitations. Changes to 【36†`sys.stdin`】, etc. are not reflected in the environment of the executed command. If command generates any output, it will be sent to the interpreter standard output stream. The C standard does not specify the meaning of the return value of the C function, so the return value of the Python function is system-dependent.
L3619: The `subprocess` module provides more powerful facilities for spawning new processes and retrieving their results; using that module is recommended to using this function. See the Replacing Older Functions with the subprocess Module section in the `subprocess` documentation for some helpful recipes.
